question: On 15 September 2025, the United States and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum to accelerate the roll-out of small modular reactors (SMRs), including by exploring maritime applications and seeking to shorten the assessment period for SMR designs to two years.1 This, in combination with other measures, increases the competitive advantage of US and UK developers over European developers.
23 Given the need for the European (maritime) industry to decarbonise and the importance of strategic autonomy and industrial competitiveness, the following questions arise: 1.

Is the Commission prepared to take immediate steps to harmonise the licensing of SMRs between Member States, including by establishing a framework for mutual recognition of national licences and by shortening the assessment period for SMR designs?
What other steps are the Commission and the European SMR Alliance taking to support European developers?

Is the Commission able to accelerate the legal basis for nuclear marine propulsion? What role can the Commission play in this context when it comes to the reform of the IMO SOLAS rules and regulations?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) The Commission is preparing a European small modular reactors (SMR) Strategy, building on the activities of the SMR Industrial Alliance, with the aim to support the fast development of SMRs in Europe.

While licensing of SMRs is a national responsibility of each Member State’s competent nuclear safety regulatory authority1, the Commission supports regulatory cooperation through the European Nuclear Safety Regulators’ Group (ENSREG).

In 2024, the ENSREG plenary meeting established a Task Force on SMRs to collect good practices from early reviews and pre-assessment of specific SMR designs and technologies, and to identify regulatory challenges to be further addressed.

The Commission supports collaboration among Member States’ regulatory authorities also through joint regulatory reviews of individual SMR designs in the pre-licensing phase and has established a grant scheme for this purpose2. The Commission supports the European SMR Industrial Alliance, whose Strategic Action Plan3 sets out actions to accelerate the deployment of SMRs in Europe by early 2030s.

The Commission is also supporting SMRs through the Euratom Research and Training Programme4. In June 2025, the Commission adopted a Nuclear Illustrative Programme (PINC)5 covering SMR technologies as a major subject for innovation. The Commission’s role is to coordinate the position of the EU Member States at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

Therefore, the Commission will continue to feed into the work of IMO aimed at the revision of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The Commission will explore the manner to enable the safe implementation of nuclear propulsion for merchant shipping, in line with its prerogatives under the Treaties.
1 In accordance with the provisions of the amended Nuclear Safety Directive: Council Directive
